title: Alpha Radiation and Alpha Decay
short_intro: Alpha radiation consists of a stream of energetic helium-4 nuclei (^4_2He) emitted spontaneously from heavy, unstable atomic nuclei. The process reduces the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2, governed by quantum mechanical tunneling through a Coulomb potential barrier.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Characteristics of alpha particles, conservation laws in radioactive decay, charge and mass changes, ionization and penetration properties, and Geiger-Nuttall law.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantum mechanical theory of alpha decay, barrier penetration probability, derivation of decay constant via Gamow's factor, and kinetic energy distribution in fine structure.

prerequisites: Binding energy per nucleon and mass defect
Quantum mechanical potential barrier and tunneling
Conservation of energy and linear momentum

concept_notes.heading: Nature and Properties of Alpha Particles
bullets: An alpha particle is identical to a doubly ionized helium atom (^4_2He^{2+}), containing two protons and two neutrons.
They possess high ionizing power due to their heavy mass and double positive charge, but low penetrating power (stopped by a thin sheet of paper or a few centimeters of air).
Alpha particles are deflected by both electric and magnetic fields, confirming their positive charge.

concept_notes.heading: Kinetic Energy and Q-Value of Decay
bullets: In a two-body decay from a stationary parent nucleus (mass M) to a daughter nucleus (mass M_d) and an alpha particle (mass M_alpha), the Q-value is given by Q = (M - M_d - M_alpha)c^2.
Due to momentum conservation, the kinetic energy of the alpha particle is slightly less than the total Q-value, sharing it with the recoiling daughter nucleus.
Alpha spectra are discrete, indicating that both parent and daughter nuclei occupy definite nuclear energy states.

concept_notes.heading: Gamow's Theory of Alpha Decay
bullets: Alpha decay is treated as a pre-formed alpha particle trapped inside a nuclear potential well, bounded by a Coulomb potential barrier.
Classically, the alpha particle lacks sufficient energy to surmount the Coulomb barrier of height V_c = \frac{1}{4piepsilon_0} \frac{2(Z-2)e^2}{R}.
Quantum mechanical tunneling allows the particle to penetrate the barrier with a finite transmission probability T.

concept_notes.heading: Geiger-Nuttall Law
bullets: An empirical relationship exists between the decay constant lambda of an alpha emitter and the range R of the emitted alpha particles in air: \log lambda = A log R + B.
A linear relationship also exists between \log lambda and the inverse square root of the alpha particle's kinetic energy.
This law is naturally explained by Gamow's barrier penetration theory.

derivations.title: Kinetic Energy of Alpha Particle from Q-Value
derivations.conditions: Stationary parent nucleus undergoing two-body alpha decay
steps: Apply conservation of linear momentum: p_\alpha + p_d = 0 \implies p_\alpha = -p_d.
Express kinetic energy in terms of momentum: E_\alpha = \frac{p_\alpha^2}{2M_\alpha} and E_d = \frac{p_d^2}{2M_d}.
Relate the energies using mass ratio: E_d = E_\alpha \left(\frac{M_\alpha}{M_d}\right).
Substitute into the total Q-value equation: Q = E_\alpha + E_d = E_\alpha \left(1 + \frac{M_\alpha}{M_d}\right) \approx E_\alpha \left(1 + \frac{4}{A-4}\right).

derivations.title: Barrier Penetration Probability (Gamow Factor)
derivations.conditions: Square-well nuclear potential with a long-range Coulomb barrier
steps: Write the WKB approximation for the transmission coefficient T through a potential barrier V(r) from classical turning point r_a to r_b.
Substitute the Coulomb potential V(r) = \frac{1}{4piepsilon_0} \frac{2(Z-2)e^2}{r} and evaluate the integral.
Express the result in terms of the fine-structure constant and velocity of the emitted alpha particle.
derivations.result: T = \exp \left[ -2 \left( \frac{2\pi Z_1 Z_2 e^2}{4piepsilon_0 \hbar v} \right) f(\frac{E}{V_c}) \right]

graphs_and_experiments.title: Nuclear Potential Well and Coulomb Barrier
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Potential energy V(r) versus radial distance r, showing the deep attractive nuclear well, the potential barrier peak, and the energy level E of the alpha particle.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that the alpha particle is bound inside by nuclear forces but escapes via quantum mechanical tunneling through the Coulomb barrier without having classical energy to go over the top.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in descriptive questions regarding why heavy nuclei emit alpha particles instead of individual nucleons.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Geiger-Nuttall Plot
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight-line graph plotting \log \lambda on the y-axis against \log R on the x-axis for different radioactive series.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that alpha emitters with higher energy (longer range R) have a much shorter half-life (larger decay constant lambda).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual interpretation of slopes and intercepts for uranium or thorium series.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Wilson Cloud Chamber Track of Alpha Particles
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Straight, dense, uniform tracks of droplets ending abruptly with a slight scatter at the end.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the heavy mass, constant specific ionization, and discrete range of monoenergetic alpha particles in a gas medium.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Identification of radiation types based on track characteristics.

solved_numericals.question: Find the kinetic energy of the alpha particle emitted in the decay of ^{226}_{88}Ra into ^{222}_{86}Rn, given that the total Q-value of the reaction is 4.87 MeV.
solution_steps: Identify the mass number of the parent nucleus: A = 226.
Use the formula relating alpha kinetic energy to Q-value: E_\alpha = Q \left( \frac{A-4}{A} \right).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the height of the Coulomb barrier for an alpha particle approaching a daughter nucleus of Uranium (Z = 90, A = 234). Assume R_0 = 1.2 fm.
solution_steps: Identify atomic number of daughter nucleus Z_d = 90, charge of alpha Z_\alpha = 2.
Calculate nuclear radius: R = R_0 A^{1/3} = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \times (234)^{1/3}.
Use Coulomb barrier formula: V_c = \frac{1}{4piepsilon_0} \frac{Z_\alpha Z_d e^2}{R}.

solved_numericals.question: The decay constant for an alpha emitter is 1.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ s}^{-1}. If the constant B in the Geiger-Nuttall relation \log \lambda = A \log R + B is 45.2 and A is -32.5, find the range R of the alpha particle in air.
solution_steps: Take the common logarithm (base 10) of lambda: \log_{10}(1.2 \times 10^{-11}) = \log_{10}(1.2) - 11 = 0.0792 - 11 = -10.9208.
Substitute into Geiger-Nuttall equation: -10.9208 = A \log R + B.
Find R by taking antilog: R = 10^{1.7268} = 53.31 \text{ cm}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the alpha particle exists as a pre-formed cluster inside the heavy nucleus prior to emission.
The potential barrier is treated as a static one-dimensional Coulomb barrier, ignoring dynamic shape deformations of the nucleus during tunneling.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Alpha particles have enough classical kinetic energy to overcome the repulsive electrostatic barrier of the nucleus.
common_misconceptions.correct: Alpha particles possess kinetic energy (4-9 MeV) much lower than the Coulomb barrier height (approx 30-35 MeV).
common_misconceptions.why: They escape exclusively via quantum mechanical tunneling, permitted by wave-particle duality.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The emitted alpha particle takes all the energy released in the decay (Q-value).
common_misconceptions.correct: The alpha particle shares the Q-value with the recoiling daughter nucleus.
common_misconceptions.why: Linear momentum must be conserved, forcing the heavy daughter nucleus to recoil in the opposite direction with a small fraction of kinetic energy.

quick_revision: Alpha emission reduces mass number A by 4 and atomic number Z by 2.
Kinetic energy of an alpha particle is always less than the Q-value due to daughter nucleus recoil.
Gamow's theory explains alpha decay successfully using quantum mechanical barrier penetration.
Geiger-Nuttall law connects decay constant directly with the range of emitted alpha particles.
